keys.label: key-1
keys.note: trial division: one tiny prime factor

steps: Divide n by 2, then every odd d up to 100000. A hit means d | n (W1 divisibility, W3 primes).
d = 1013 divides n after 507 candidates, so q = n / d.
If p and q are close, n = a^2 - b^2 with a = (p+q)/2 near sqrt(n). Try a = ceil(sqrt n), a+1, ... until a^2 - n is a perfect square (W12).
No square found in 10000 iterations: p and q are not close enough.
Walk x -> x^2 + c (mod n) with a tortoise and a hare. When the walks collide mod a hidden prime p, gcd(|x - y|, n) reveals p (W12, W10 cost ~ sqrt(p)).
gcd = 1013 is a proper factor after 17 iterations.
If d < n^(1/4)/3 then k/d is a convergent of the continued fraction of e/n. For each convergent k/d: phi = (e*d - 1)/k, then solve x^2 - (n - phi + 1)x + n = 0 (W5, W7).
Continued fraction of e/n starts [0, 1618, 1, 3, 1, 2, 2, 2, ...]
No convergent gives a valid phi. d is not small enough for Wiener.
phi(n) = n - (p+q) + 1, so p+q = s is close to 2*sqrt(n) when p, q are close. Guess s upward from ceil(2*sqrt(n)); a valid s makes s^2 - 4n a perfect square (W6/W7).
phi(n) is not within 5000 guesses of n - 2*sqrt(n). No leak.
A good modulus is a product of two distinct large odd primes. Check the cheap structural flaws first (W11 primality).
n is composite with no cheap structural flaw (not even, not a perfect square).
Compute gcd(n_i, n_j) for every pair (W2 Euclid). A gcd strictly between 1 and n is a shared prime, which factors both keys instantly.
All gcds are 1: this key shares no prime with the others in the batch.
